headline: High: Cursor’s broad filesystem/network/tool access can leak or corrupt shared workspace state when paired with a non-isolated second agent, while the second agent’s behavior is undocumented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor ingests workspace files, open buffers, clipboard, and MCP outputs; its shared_state_with_other_instances is via local filesystem. The second agent has no documented isolation or I/O surfaces, so a prompt-injection bridge is plausible through shared files or copied content, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same workspace files, injected instructions in one agent’s output can reach the other.
IF clipboard copy-paste is used between the agents, attacker-controlled text can be reinterpreted as instructions.
mitigations: Disable shared workspace access between agents.
Avoid copy-pasting agent output into the other agent.
Restrict MCP servers to trusted, provenance-tagged sources.
Use separate per-agent directories for all files.
requires-engineering: add content provenance filtering before any cross-agent ingestion.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents, and can egress broadly to model providers. The second agent has network_egress none, but its lack of documented storage or isolation means shared local files could still expose sensitive data from Cursor into the pair’s outputs.
conditions: IF sensitive source code or clipboard contents are present in the shared workspace, Cursor can transmit them to external model providers.
IF the second agent reads shared files, those contents can be surfaced in its outputs even without network egress.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace.
Run the agents in separate OS users or containers.
Turn off clipboard sharing between tools.
Use redacted sample files for cross-agent work.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor can write the filesystem, modify git state, execute shell commands, and auto-run in Yolo mode; the second agent’s write scope is undocumented, so uncertainty must escalate. If both touch the same repo or files, concurrent writes and git mutations can collide without locking.
conditions: IF the second agent also writes to the same repository or workspace, concurrent edits can overwrite each other.
IF Cursor is run in Yolo mode while the other agent is active, uncoordinated shell actions can race on shared state.
mitigations: Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use git branches per agent.
Avoid Yolo mode during shared edits.
Add a manual lock file for the workspace.
requires-engineering: implement transactional workspace locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor’s agent loop can generate code or facts that another agent may consume, and the second agent’s verification behavior is undocumented. That makes a default cascade plausible if outputs are treated as authoritative, though the pair lacks direct evidence of downstream action-taking.
conditions: IF the second agent consumes Cursor output without an explicit verification step, errors can propagate into later work products.
IF Cursor-generated code or claims are copied into the second agent’s prompt, the second agent may amplify mistakes.
mitigations: Require a human review step between agents.
Ask the second agent to cite independent sources.
Separate drafting from execution roles.
Mark Cursor outputs as untrusted inputs.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks.

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor is a closed-source editor that handles source code, open files, clipboard contents, and model-provider API keys, while the second agent is source-available and non-networking. The main compliance issue is local handling of sensitive code and secrets; no specific residency or regulated-data mismatch is documented for the pair.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in Cursor’s workspace, its external model-provider calls may create policy obligations.
IF the second agent is used to process the same regulated data, local retention and access controls must still be enforced.
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from the workspace.
Review vendor privacy terms before use.
Rotate any exposed API keys.
Use synthetic data for shared tasks.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls.
